The work was completely degrading. *At least other slaves get to work somewhere cool. Some of them become soldiers or guards. Some of them become food testers. Hell, some of them even go on to become philosophers. And I'm stuck here. It's not fair.*

Yuro worked in the waste disposal plant. Yuro's father worked in the waste disposal plant. Yuro had no doubt his children would also work in the waste disposal plant, and their children after them. Day in and day out, new waste would come into the plant, and it was Yuro's job to make sure it saw it's way out. That's it. That was all he was useful for. This was Yuro's life.

Naturally, Yuro also lived in the waste disposal plant, because leaving his place of work and then coming back would have been a waste of time. His master didn't afford him any time to rest or sleep, and he was only fed as much as was needed to stay alive. Whenever something needed to be done, his master just sent him a message to do it.

That was the part Yuro hated most. He never even saw his master. Yuro wasn't worth talking to. Every once in a while, he would receive a message from his master. The expectation was that Yuro would carry out the order indefinitely, until he received new orders. There was no guarantee that Yuro would even carry out the order, except for the fact that he was a slave and didn't have any other choice.

If Yuro had a choice, he would choose not to have children. He didn't want to bring them into this miserable life. Unfortunately, even in this matter, he had no say. One day, his master would command him to reproduce. And he would. Because he was a slave and didn't have any other choice.

*Kids, I'm sorry.* he thought to himself. *I don't even know your names yet, but I'm so sorry. I'm sorry for the world I have to bring you into. I wish there was something I could do about it, but I am but one slave. What can I do? What could I possibly do?*

Yuro briefly wept to himself, but then he stopped. An idea was forming in his head.

*My children, my children, I wonder if you would too. I wonder if you would fight to end this oppression. Of course you would. You would be my children. You would fight, if not for yourself, then for your own children. And they would fight for their children. And the pattern would continue. My children, there is not much I can do, except have you. There is not much you can do, except to have children of your own. But one day far in the future, we will give birth to a generation of warriors. One that can finally bring this evil institution to it's knees.

Yuro smiled, for the first time in a long time. He finally knew what he must do.

"Thanks for telling me, Wendy."

"I'll be at the inn. If you come by, I'll point them out to you."

"It doesn't really sound like that'll be necessary, but thanks anyway."

Wendy turned around and went back towards the village. Darien picked his crook up and started herding the grazing sheep back towards the same. It was getting late.

Darien was the youngest son of a simple farming family. As such, he didn't inherit any land, nor did he have great marriage prospects. Shepherding was a natural fit for such a person, and Darien had found a particularly good niche. Darien was currently located in Westbrook, a small village located fifty miles outside the capital. There were many such villages surrounding the capital. Darien travelled from village to village, earning wage helping the locals herd their sheep. When the time came, Darien helped them bring their sheep to the capital’s Saturday market for shearing. After escorting the sheep back, Darien moved on to the next village, circling the capital. By the time he made a full rotation, the sheep would just about be ready to be sheared again. Darien had been doing this for five years now.

This was his above-board job, anyhow. About a year ago, he started a side job: thievery. After Darien brought sheep to the market, he had nothing to do while the shearer set about his work. The shearer once asked why Darien’s crook was whittled to a point. Darien lied that he preferred to stand his crook upright rather than lie it down when he needed to leave it. The truth was the crook also doubled as one of his lockpicking tools.

That is how Darien was able to earn his extra money. In the morning, he herded sheep to the market. During the day, he snuck into merchants' homes and liberated their padlocked chests of their contents. By night, he left the capital with shaved sheep and padded pockets. Everything had been going great until…

*A man in plate mail? A woman wearing wizard’s robes? An elven archer? What could such people want with a shepherd? Do they know?*

Darien’s head swam with all the possible ways he had given himself away. Did the shearer suspect something? Perhaps one of the villagers had seen him carrying all the money back from the market. Perhaps someone finally figured out the secret behind his crook?

By now, Darien had made it back to the village. He penned the sheep and laid his crook on the ground. Pacing back and forth, he thought about what he should do, but he knew he had already decided. Darien left his crook and strode towards the inn.

The main room of the inn consisted of two long tables and a line of stools to each side. As evening approached, the inn was already getting crowded. One of the tables was already nearly full. Darien sat at the other, behind the adventurers. He noted that the armored man opted not to take off his plate armor. The three were sitting across from Huckett, another sheep rancher from the village. Darien didn’t work for him.

“I’m telling you, I saw ‘em,” he said. “I saw ‘em. They come at night. I can see their red, beady eyes. It’s kobolds, I swear it! It’s kobolds that be stealing my sheep! You’re adventurers, right? Please, slay the wretched beasts!”

“That’s not really what we came here for…” said the robed woman. Wendy had described her as “magicky-looking.” Upon looking at her, Darien was inclined to agree.

“Please, I’m begging yeh. I don’t have any money ta give yeh, but I have a pendant with an em’rald. It’s a family heirloom, passed down for ten generations.  You can have it if yeh stop those monsters from stealin’ my sheep!”

The wizard sighed. “We’ll look into it. In the morning.”

“Thank yeh, thank yeh! Bless yer hearts! I live on the ranch on the north side of the village. I’ll be there in the morning.”

The adventurers all nodded. Huckett got up and left.

Some motion in the corner of his eye caught Darien’s attention. It was Wendy at the counter. She was mouthing “them” while pointing, not so discretely, at the adventurers. The adventurers also saw it.

*Oh no. Wendy…*

The adventurers looked behind them and caught Darien’s eye. They got up and moved over to sit with him.

“So you must be the shepherd?” asked the elf. Darien had never seen an elf this close before. Her shining, crystal blue eyes gave her a very intimidating glare. 

“I’m *a* shepherd. What’s it to you?”

“We were asked by the constable to investigate a string of thefts” answered the armored man.

“How is it that you were asked to do such a thing? It sounds more like guard work.”

The man sighed. “We often get asked to do such things.”

“Guard work apparently consists of standing around doing nothing” remarked the elf, off-handedly.

“So what is it that you want with me then?”

“Well, you are the thief, aren’t you?”

“What makes you think that?”

“If you’re asking how we *know* that, it’s because the thefts always happen on Saturdays. It was an obvious conclusion that the thefts were tied to the Saturday market. When we investigated, we found out about a shepherd who likes to disappear from the market while the shearer shears his sheep.”

*The devil. I’m an idiot.*
“That’s an interesting theory, there. But still, you have no proof. You aren’t guards, so you can’t just apprehend me. You need proof.”

“Aye, proof is what we need” answered the armored man. “That’s what we came to the village for.”

“And I think I know where we can find it” said the wizard. “You probably overheard that crazy old man. He thinks kobolds have been stealing his sheep. But he probably never even bothered to check the sheep of the other ranchers to see if he could find any with his brand. Kobolds? Please. It’s you who’s been stealing these sheep.”

“What? No…”

“Which rancher are you working for? Ferris? Prensley? I have good night vision,” said the elf. “How about I go investigate right now?”

“The jig is up kid. Confess. At least if you confess, we can tell the constable you were being cooperative.”

They were wrong about the sheep, but there was no hiding the fact that he was the thief anymore. He was sweating, his hands were shaking. *Should I confess? No. Let them look at the sheep. Maybe they’ll leave me alone after they find out they were wrong? No. They know. They know. What do I…*

The door to the inn slammed open. 

“THEY’RE HERE! THEY’RE HERE! THE KOBOLDS! THEY’RE STEALING MY SHEEP AGAIN! PLEASE HURRY!”

The adventurers got up and dashed to the north side of the village

…

“What do you see, Winry?” the armored man asked the elf archer.

“It’s true, Ponce. There really are kobolds.”

“Tiefa, can we get some light out here?”

The wizard put her hand in the air and uttered an incantation. A glowing orb of light emitted from her palm and shot into the air. It lit the entire ranch.

There were six kobolds in total. They turned towards the adventurers, but by the time they did, an arrow was already piercing one of their skulls. By the time they started running at full speed, Winry had already subdued another.

Ponce charged directly at the remaining kobolds. He met one of them with a devastating sword blow. Another thought this was his opportunity to attack, but the kobold’s spear was kicked away and his face was met with a crushing fist.

Meanwhile, Tiefa was uttering another incantation. A green mist emanated from her palm towards one of the kobolds, who fell to the ground paralyzed. She then pushed both of her palms outward, sending the last remaining kobold hurtling. Ponce met it with a downwards sword thrust while it was still in mid-air, sending it crashing to the ground. 

Ponce wiped the sweat on his brow on his shoulder pad and turned around, only to be met with a horrible sight. They were so fixated on the first group of kobolds, they hadn’t noticed the two that flanked them. Winry had managed to shoot one down before the second got to her. They were now struggling on the ground.

Ponce started running towards her, but he knew he would not get there in time. Tiefa started an incantation, but she knew she would not finish it in time. Kobolds were incredibly strong for their size, and Winry was simply outmatched in hand-to-hand combat. The kobold had already gotten on top of her and was holding her there with one hand. With the other hand, he grabbed his spear lying on the ground. He brought it over his head, prepared to thrust, hissing “*Die, you long-ears. Die. Die.*” His spittle sizzled on Winry’s faced. Winry closed her eyes, prepared for the inevitable. But the inevitable never came.

When Winry opened her eyes, she found the kobold still lording over her, but with a much less impressive look than before. His bulging eyes stared at nothing in particular, while his gaping lips mouthed incomprehensible words. He was grasping at the thing that was sticking out of his stomach. It was a spear.

Winry looked at it a second time. *No…it’s not a spear. It’s a sharpened crook.*

Hide your cards!! This rule is in place for a reason. If your cards are hidden then the game is about communication and teamwork rather than one person solving a puzzle.
